passage:
Monday. Vandana gave a perfect imitation of the maths teacher's cough as he turned to the board, and the class roared. Bhupen banged his desk and shouted, “Do it again!” She did.
Wednesday. The test papers came back. Vandana held hers up. “Nineteen out of fifty! I'm a legend!” Twenty voices cheered. Only the girl beside her, who had scored the same, said nothing and looked down.
Friday. The teacher asked her to stay behind. “Your timing is very good,” he said quietly. “I'd like it in the debate club. And come on Thursdays after school. We'll go through the sums together.” Vandana laughed, but her hands gripped her bag.

qa.q: What did Vandana say when she held up her test paper on Wednesday?
qa.a: Vandana said, “Nineteen out of fifty! I'm a legend!”

qa.q: Why might Vandana joke loudly about her score?
qa.a: Vandana seems to hide worry about being seen as weak in studies, and the class's cheering gives her status when the score might have brought shame.

qa.q: What did the teacher do on Friday that avoided humiliating Vandana?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to Vandana privately, praised her timing, offered the debate club and offered help with the sums on Thursdays, without shaming her in front of the class.

qa.q: What might the girl beside Vandana have been feeling when she scored the same and looked down?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and alone with the same mark, without a joke to hide behind while the others cheered.

grounding: A teenager makes jokes to gain laughs and status while covering worry about studies, the class cheers, and the teacher handles it privately without humiliation.

passage: “Come and sit, Rehan,” said Uncle Wasim, tapping the bench. “I'll tell you about Sumit Sir.” When I was fifteen I was the class clown. The back bench chanted my name whenever I did a voice. Really I couldn't follow the algebra and was scared everyone would find out. One day I turned the teacher's chalk-dust cough into a song. The whole class howled. Sumit Sir didn't shout. He said, “Wasim, keep that voice for after the bell. Come to my desk at lunch.” At his desk he said, “You are funny and you are lost. Let's fix the second one.” The back bench was quiet, and later I noticed a few of them were lost too.

qa.q: Who did the back bench chant when Wasim did a voice?
qa.a: The back bench chanted Wasim's name whenever he did a voice.

qa.q: Why was Wasim so keen to make the class laugh?
qa.a: Wasim seems to have been scared that everyone would find out he could not follow the algebra, and the laughter gave him standing in place of marks.

qa.q: What did Sumit Sir do that helped Wasim without embarrassing him?
qa.a: Sumit Sir did not shout in front of the class, asked Wasim to come to his desk at lunch, named both the humour and the difficulty, and offered to work on the difficulty.

qa.q: What might the students on the back bench have felt when Sumit Sir spoke to Wasim?
qa.a: They may have felt caught out, since they had been encouraging Wasim, and later some noticed they were lost too, which suggests the chanting had covered worry for them as well.

grounding: A teenager clowns for laughs and status to hide worry about studies, the class encourages it, and the teacher handles it without humiliation.
